prompt: Who makes the phones that run iOS?

choices.text: Google, under the Android Open Source Project
choices.why: The Android Open Source Project is Android's source. iOS is Apple's.

choices.text: Any manufacturer that licenses it from Apple
choices.why: Apple does not license iOS to other manufacturers; that model is Android's.

choices.text: Apple, and nobody else
choices.why: Right. One company writes the system and makes every device it runs on.

choices.text: Apple designs them and phone makers build them under several brands
choices.why: There is one brand of iPhone. Several brands on one system is how Android works.

prompt: Why does an Android app declare a minimum SDK and support a range of system versions at once?

choices.text: Manufacturers decide when, or whether, a phone gets a new Android
choices.why: Right. Phones in use run many versions at once, so the app has to as well.

choices.text: Because Google Play refuses apps for the newest version
choices.why: The range is not a store rule. It follows from how updates reach phones.

choices.text: Kotlin compiles to a different program for each version
choices.why: One build runs on every version from the minimum up; the compiler is not the reason.

choices.text: Users choose which Android version to install
choices.why: The user takes what the manufacturer ships, and that is the point.

prompt: Match each platform's language and toolkit.
A student has a Windows laptop and no Mac. Which of these can they not do on it?

choices.text: Run Android Studio
choices.why: Android Studio runs on Windows, macOS and Linux.

choices.text: Write Kotlin
choices.why: Kotlin and its compiler run on any computer with a Java Development Kit.

choices.text: Run this course's programs
choices.why: They are TypeScript on Node.js, which runs in WSL on Windows.

choices.text: Build an iOS app with Xcode
choices.why: Right. Xcode runs on macOS alone.

prompt: Which of these is a constraint the system enforces rather than a design convention?

choices.text: Tabs at the bottom of the screen on iOS
choices.why: That is the Human Interface Guidelines' convention; an app can place tabs elsewhere and still run.

choices.text: The system back action every Android app has to answer
choices.why: Right. The user can always press back, whatever the app's designer decided.

choices.text: A floating button for the main action in Material Design
choices.why: A design guide recommends it; nothing stops an app from omitting it.

choices.text: Rounded switches on iOS and flat ones on Android
choices.why: How a switch looks is the design guide's business, not the system's.

prompt: A friend wants to try your app on their phone before it is in any store. How does that differ between the platforms?

choices.text: Both need the app to pass the store's review before any phone can run it
choices.why: An Android app can be installed from a file with no review at all.

choices.text: Android installs a file; iPhone needs Apple's TestFlight
choices.why: Right. An iPhone runs only apps signed through Apple.

choices.text: Neither allows it; testing happens on emulators
choices.why: Both have a way to put a test build on a real phone.

choices.text: On iOS you send the file; Android needs Google's test service
choices.why: It is the other way round.

prompt: Which of these hold on both Android and iOS? Choose every one that does.

choices.text: The system can kill the app's process when it decides to
choices.why: Right. Lessons 4 and 5 are about it.

choices.text: A refused permission can stay refused for good
choices.why: Right. Lesson 12 shows how each platform says it.

choices.text: A back action provided by the system
choices.why: Android has one; an iPhone does not.

choices.text: Each app's storage is a sandbox other apps cannot read
choices.why: Right. Lesson 16 opens it.

prompt: A designer proposes an iOS app with tabs at the top, like an older Android app. What is the honest answer?

choices.text: iOS will refuse to draw tabs there
choices.why: Nothing in the system forbids it; tab placement is a convention.

choices.text: App Review rejects any app that does not follow the guidelines exactly
choices.why: Review rejects for many reasons, and a tab bar's position is not a rule it enforces in that way.

choices.text: It works only if the app is written in Swift
choices.why: The language has nothing to do with where tabs go.

choices.text: It will work, and iPhone users will find it unfamiliar
choices.why: Right. A convention broken costs familiarity, not function.

prompt: What does this course ask you to install on your computer?

choices.text: Node.js 22, git and a text editor
choices.why: Right. Every program in the course is TypeScript run by Node.js.

choices.text: Android Studio and Xcode
choices.why: Neither: the courses after the fork bring those in.

choices.text: An Android emulator, so the planner has a screen
choices.why: The planner has no screen in this course, on purpose.

choices.text: Expo, and a phone with the Expo Go app
choices.why: That is the React Native route, after the fork.

prompt: A lesson shows the same idea in Kotlin, Swift and React Native. What does the course say about those fragments?

choices.text: They were compiled on all three platforms when the course was recorded
choices.why: They were not compiled or run; the lesson says so beside each one.

choices.text: You type them in and run them as part of the exercises
choices.why: You run TypeScript on Node.js here; the platform code is for the courses after the fork.

choices.text: They come from each platform's documentation and were not run
choices.why: Right. You read them to recognise the idea in three spellings.

choices.text: Only the React Native one is real code
choices.why: All three are real code from documentation, and none was run.

prompt: Match each later course with what it needs beyond Node.js and git.

pairs.right: a Mac with Xcode for anything that draws a screen
Android Studio, its SDK, and an emulator or a phone
a Java Development Kit 21 and Gradle
an account with each store, and they charge

prompt: A student without a Mac must choose a route at the fork. Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: Android and React Native are practised fully; ios-apps is mostly read
choices.why: Right. That is the one route tied to a particular computer.

choices.text: No route works without a Mac, because every app is eventually built on one
choices.why: Android Studio and Node.js run on Windows and Linux; only the iOS toolchain is tied to macOS.

choices.text: Swift cannot be installed at all without a Mac
choices.why: The Swift toolchain installs on Linux; it is Xcode and the screens that need macOS.

choices.text: React Native needs a Mac for its JavaScript to run
choices.why: Node.js and Expo run on any computer.

prompt: Why does this course need Node.js 22.18 or later, and records on 22.22.0?

choices.text: 22.22.0 is the first version that includes npm
choices.why: npm has shipped with Node.js for many years.

choices.text: Older versions cannot run JavaScript modules
choices.why: Modules ran long before 22.18; TypeScript files did not, without a flag.

choices.text: From 22.18, node runs a .ts file directly by stripping its types
choices.why: Right. No compiler and no build step.

choices.text: Earlier versions of Node.js 22 do not install or run on Ubuntu 24.04
choices.why: They run; the lesson shows 22.17.0 running there and refusing the .ts file.

prompt: After installing Node.js into ~/.local/node, `node --version` in the same terminal fails. What is the fix the lesson gives?

choices.text: Install Node.js again from your system's packages
choices.why: That makes a second copy, which is its own problem.

choices.text: Open a new terminal, which reads PATH when it starts
choices.why: Right. The old terminal decided its PATH before the folder existed.

choices.text: Run the tar command a second time
choices.why: The files are already there; the shell is not looking in that folder yet.

choices.text: Reboot the computer
choices.why: It works, and is far more than is needed.

prompt: Which path does the lesson recommend, and why?

choices.text: Online, because it costs nothing
choices.why: It costs nothing on your computer and draws on a monthly allowance that is charged past its end.

choices.text: Installed, because Node.js needs administrator rights to run
choices.why: It runs as an ordinary user, from your home folder.

choices.text: A virtual machine, because the programs need a phone emulator
choices.why: Nothing in this course needs an emulator.

choices.text: Installed: one folder in your home, nothing else touched
choices.why: Right. It is the cheapest of the three and matches the transcripts on Linux.

prompt: In the lesson's plan, how many minutes are planned for the week of Monday 19 October 2026?
Why is session s4 left out of the week's total?

choices.text: It is not done yet
choices.why: s3 is not done either, and it counts towards the minutes planned.

choices.text: Its course does not exist
choices.why: Its course is mobile, which exists; addSession would have refused it otherwise.

choices.text: Its date, 27 October, falls in the following week
choices.why: Right. mondayOf gives 26 October for it, not 19.

choices.text: weekTotal ignores sessions longer than 40 minutes
choices.why: Nothing filters by length; s3 is 60 minutes and counts.

prompt: weekTotal takes today as an argument instead of reading the clock. What does that buy?

choices.text: The same plan always gives the same answer
choices.why: Right. So your run matches the transcript on any day, and a test can pin the result.

choices.text: It works in every time zone, which reading the clock does not
choices.why: The time zone is handled by reading dates at noon UTC, a separate decision.

choices.text: It runs faster, because reading the clock is slow
choices.why: Reading the clock costs next to nothing; speed is not the reason.

choices.text: Node.js cannot read the clock in a .ts file
choices.why: It can; Date works the same in a stripped .ts file.

prompt: A session points at its course by the course's ___, so renaming a course loses nothing.
Node.js prints `Cannot find module '/home/ana/week.ts'`, and the file is in ~/planner. What happened?

choices.text: The node that the terminal found first is older than 22.18
choices.why: An old Node.js finds the file and refuses its extension, with a different message.

choices.text: week.ts has a syntax error
choices.why: A syntax error is reported after the file is found; this one was never found.

choices.text: package.json is missing "type": "module"
choices.why: That gives a warning, and the program still runs.

choices.text: The terminal was in the home folder, not in ~/planner
choices.why: Right. node looks for the file relative to where the terminal is.

prompt: Match each message with its cause.

pairs.right: a Node.js older than 22.18 was found first

pairs.left: TypeScript enum is not supported in strip-only mode
pairs.right: syntax that is more than a type

prompt: Why does node refuse an enum but accept `type Level = "beginner" | "advanced"`?

choices.text: Enums were removed from TypeScript
choices.why: TypeScript still has them; a compiler turns them into code.

choices.text: An enum is a real object at run time
choices.why: Right. Deleting it would break the program, while a union of strings is only a type and strips away cleanly.

choices.text: Node.js accepts enums only in .mts files
choices.why: The extension changes nothing; strip-only mode refuses them everywhere.

choices.text: The enum was declared before the type it uses
choices.why: Order is not the issue; the message names the construct itself.

prompt: Put the first steps of the planner project in order.
items: make the folder ~/planner and cd into it

prompt: A program prints the right answer and a warning under it. What does the lesson advise?

choices.text: Ignore it, since the answer is right
choices.why: It works today, and old warnings hide the next new one.

choices.text: Fix exactly what it names
choices.why: Right. Then the next warning is easy to see, and this one even says which line to add and where.

choices.text: Run node with a flag that hides every warning it prints
choices.why: That hides this warning and every later one, including the one that matters.

choices.text: Reinstall Node.js
choices.why: Nothing is wrong with the installation; the project's package.json lost a line.
